supporting_evidence: Dense sweeps, targeted randomized rows, fresh-editor rows, and volatility plots reproduce the shape.
disconfirming_evidence: The drop survives multiple run shapes and does not depend on one graph or one aggregate.
surviving_claim: The cliff is a real benchmark artifact.
next_decisive_observation: None unless a future helper/browser revision changes the row ordering.

supporting_evidence: Held-key and complete-keypress/tap rows have different delay curves under matched conditions.
disconfirming_evidence: Observed physical hold duration and post-keyup gap do not explain the whole split.
surviving_claim: The held-key helper path is a different metric from keypress-then-wait.
next_decisive_observation: Repeat exact CI helper rows only if the suite changes helper family or Playwright semantics.

supporting_evidence: Persistence markers, timer rewrites, and marker/no-op/raw-action controls put the transition near the rich-text persistence boundary.
disconfirming_evidence: Simple claims that any timer, raw store action, or direct callback work explains the drop are rejected.
surviving_claim: Persistence timing is an ordering marker for the held-key transition.
next_decisive_observation: Per-retained-key task/runtime joins if the claim expands from ordering marker to exact mechanism.

theory: Timer callback shifts work out of next key
supporting_evidence: The timer fires near the transition, which made this theory tempting.
disconfirming_evidence: The current artifacts do not show that the callback performs work that would otherwise be charged to the next key, and several store-work controls reject that shortcut.
surviving_claim: Do not use this as a causal explanation; keep the wording at ordering marker.
next_decisive_observation: A joined task trace showing callback work, next-key work, and counterfactual work placement would be required.

supporting_evidence: Chrome EventDispatch slices move with the cliff.
disconfirming_evidence: Firefox preserves a similar controlled dip, so Chrome-only accounting is too narrow.
surviving_claim: Chrome EventDispatch is one measured endpoint, not the whole cause.
next_decisive_observation: Same-grid browser/runtime sidecar only if naming browser-specific mechanisms matters.

theory: Complete-keypress or human typing has the same 1000ms cliff
supporting_evidence: Complete-keypress/tap rows provide the direct comparison.
disconfirming_evidence: Tap and keypress-then-wait rows do not reproduce the held-key curve as the same metric.
surviving_claim: The current cliff claim is held-key specific.
next_decisive_observation: Representative workload replay if product typing behavior is the claim.

theory: Ordinary sleep or queued-JS drain is sufficient
supporting_evidence: Longer post-keyup waits and ordinary waits were plausible after the first runtime-checkpoint rows.
disconfirming_evidence: Raw CDP ordinary waits through multi-second delays do not reproduce the same fast class.
surviving_claim: Elapsed rest time by itself is insufficient.
next_decisive_observation: No more ordinary-wait extensions unless a browser/helper revision changes the row ordering.

theory: React render or post-EventDispatch work causes the cliff
supporting_evidence: React/render work exists after input and can affect whole-cycle latency.
disconfirming_evidence: The main movement is already inside the EventDispatch/input slice; post-EventDispatch visual/render tails are too small for primary cliff causality.
surviving_claim: React profiling is useful only for residual ownership after a source change.
next_decisive_observation: Matched profiler/unprofiled rows only after a selector or store-notification patch changes the fanout shape.

theory: Broad data subscriber fanout supplies much of the editable-scale cost
supporting_evidence: Source spans and listener wrapper audits identify broad block-editor/root subscriber fanout.
disconfirming_evidence: Single-owner and selector-body-only explanations are rejected; compatibility still constrains fixes.
surviving_claim: Fanout is a source-cost target, not the lower-level runtime mechanism.
next_decisive_observation: Behavior-gated selector/source-span prototype and public compatibility fixtures.

theory: Runtime checkpoint/browser scheduler state separates fast and slow rows
supporting_evidence: Runtime-repeat and checkpoint controls preserve a dose response below ordinary JS rows.
disconfirming_evidence: Elapsed wait, DOM payload, generic task/frame checkpoint, and native-only explanations are not enough.
surviving_claim: An unnamed browser/runtime state remains plausible.
next_decisive_observation: Trace-off protocol sidecar with key-window joins and observer-on/off ordering controls.

theory: CPU/QoS or power state modulates absolute latency
supporting_evidence: External CPU and taskpolicy/QoS controls move absolute latency and preserve several class orderings.
disconfirming_evidence: Nice/taskpolicy machinery in general and CPU burn anywhere are too broad.
surviving_claim: A narrower system-state influence is plausible but unnamed.
next_decisive_observation: Accepted retained-key sidecar followed by root powermetrics or trace counters.

theory: Startup wait determines the typing result
supporting_evidence: Startup-wait matrices and per-key rows directly test waiting before measurement.
disconfirming_evidence: Added startup waits do not improve retained q50 stability enough to justify them under the current typing metric.
surviving_claim: Initial-key/user-idle latency is a separate metric from retained typing q50.
next_decisive_observation: CI topology artifact only if wait removal affects readiness, failures, resources, or first-key tails.

theory: Pattern fixed wait can be removed everywhere from local q50 alone
supporting_evidence: Local matrices find shorter waits and 0ms candidates in some paths.
disconfirming_evidence: Site Editor, Post Editor, preview/canvas, resources, actionability, and container/CI topology are different contracts.
surviving_claim: Some fixed waits are likely reducible, but rollout is gated by readiness and topology.
next_decisive_observation: Real Performance Tests artifact retaining failures, resources, preview/canvas, run order, and environment metadata.

theory: Store subscriber partition is safe because timing improves
supporting_evidence: Marker fanout creates a large timing target.
disconfirming_evidence: Public store subscription, persistence selector behavior, dynamic dependencies, and plugin compatibility are semantic gates.
surviving_claim: Timing can motivate a prototype, but not prove a data-layer API change.
next_decisive_observation: Public compatibility matrix plus marker-only listener-collapse artifact.
